MA342 overview

MA342 Topic Guide

Compactness

Convert arbitrary open covers into finite arguments.

Purpose

State compactness exactly, disprove it with a topology-valid cover, and combine it with Hausdorff separation.Exam use: In 2025/26, Q2(d) asks for the definition and non-compactness of the lower-limit line for 5 marks, while Q2(e) asks for the compact-subspace-of-Hausdorff closedness proof for 5 marks.

Question plan

  1. Begin with an arbitrary open cover.
  2. When disproving compactness, verify that every member of the proposed cover is open in the stated topology.
  3. When compactness meets Hausdorffness, separate one external point from every point of the compact subspace and then choose finitely many separations.
  4. Question interpretation: “Is it compact?” needs a conclusion and proof; “show compact implies closed” requires the Hausdorff hypothesis at the point-separation step.

Definitions

X is compact iff every open cover of X has a finite subcover. Closed subsets of compact spaces and continuous images of compact spaces are compact. Compact subspaces of Hausdorff spaces are closed. In Euclidean space, compactness is equivalent to closedness and boundedness by Heine–Borel.Rapid recall: To disprove compactness, one explicit open cover with no finite subcover is enough; to turn compact into closed, add Hausdorff separation.

Proof method

Let A be compact in Hausdorff X and x∉A. For each a∈A choose disjoint open Ua containing a and Va containing x. Compactness reduces {Ua} to Ua1,…,Uan. Then V=Va1∩⋯∩Van is an open neighbourhood of x disjoint from A. Thus X\A is open.Exam workflow: Use Hausdorffness point-by-point, compactness exactly once to make the family finite, and only then take the finite intersection around x.

Worked simple example

{0}∪{1/n:n≥1} is compact in R because it is closed and bounded; equivalently, use Heine–Borel.

Medium/hard paper-style synthesis

The lower-limit real line Rℓ is not compact. The basic-open sets Un=[n,n+1), n∈Z, cover R. Any finite subfamily covers only a bounded union of these intervals and therefore misses all sufficiently large positive and negative real numbers. Hence this open cover has no finite subcover.

Graduated exam bridges

1. Foundation: Why is the Cantor set compact Hausdorff? Check: it is closed in compact [0,1], and it inherits Hausdorffness from R.

2. Exam style: Prove a closed F⊆X is compact when X is compact. Check: add X\F to an arbitrary cover of F.

Hard paper-style synthesis

If X is compact, Y Hausdorff and f:X→Y continuous and bijective, then f is a homeomorphism. For closed F⊆X, F is compact, so f(F) is compact and therefore closed in Hausdorff Y. Thus f is closed, which makes f-1 continuous.

Practice question - lower-limit and Hausdorff compactness [10 marks]

Inspired by: MA342 2025/26 Q2(d-e). Task. (a) Define compactness and decide, with justification, whether the lower-limit real line Rℓ is compact. [5 marks] (b) Let A be a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space X. Show that A is closed in X. [5 marks]

Demand diagnosis and fastest route: use the integer-indexed half-open cover for (a); for (b), separate a fixed x∉A from each a∈A and use compactness to retain only finitely many separating neighbourhoods.

Worked answer: A space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. In Rℓ, {[n,n+1):n∈Z} is an open cover, but every finite subfamily has bounded union and cannot cover R, so Rℓ is not compact. For (b), fix x∈X\A. For each a∈A, Hausdorffness gives disjoint open sets Ua∋a and Va∋x. Compactness supplies a finite cover A⊆Ua1∪⋯∪Uan. The open set V=Va1∩⋯∩Van contains x and is disjoint from A. Hence every x∈X\A has an open neighbourhood in X\A, so A is closed.

Topic-specific trap: an infinite intersection of the Va need not be open; compactness is what reduces it to a finite intersection.

Mistakes

  • Choosing a finite cover instead of proving a finite subcover of an arbitrary cover.
  • Using Heine–Borel outside Euclidean space.
  • Forgetting closedness in the closed-subset theorem.
  • Recovery rule: A sequence argument is not automatically available in an arbitrary topological space; use open covers unless sequential compactness has been established.

Checklist

  • I can state the open-cover definition.
  • I can give a noncompact open-cover counterexample.
  • I can reproduce the closed-subset proof.
  • I can prove a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space is closed.
  • Final 60-second audit: The cover is arbitrary when proving compactness, explicit when disproving it, and every theorem hypothesis is named.

The 2025/26 paper directly tests the definition and lower-limit non-compactness in Q2(d), compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces in Q2(e), compactness of the Cantor set in Q4(a), and compactness as a quotient obstruction in Q4(d).
